A learner of Spanish (own language English) just revised a piece for Email to a language school. These are the parts that changed:
1. They first wrote: "Primero, prefiero una habitación con familia / un piso compartido, no sé cual es mejor para aprender. ¿Es el piso cerca de la escuela?"
   It ended as: "Primero, prefiero un piso compartido con otra gente para aprender. ¿Queda el piso cerca de la escuela?"
   What was wrong: The slash still presents two options he has not chosen, and the sentence says he does not know which is better. The reader cannot tell what accommodation to arrange, and the following question about 'el piso' assumes a flat.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: compartido: A flat share is the normal term here for a flat you share with others. Writing only 'un piso' would leave out the 'with other people' part of what he means. / con otra gente: Spells out who he would share with. 'Compartido' alone can be read loosely, so this makes clear he means housemates, not a room with a family. / para aprender: Keeps his own reason for the choice without adding a claim he has not made. 'Para aprender mejor' would say the flat is better for learning, which he did not say. / queda: Spanish asks where something is with 'quedar'. Writing '¿Es el piso cerca…?' copies the English 'is it near', which a Spanish speaker would not say.
2. They first wrote: "Tercero, soy vegetariano (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat) y espero que la familia puede cocinar algo para mí."
   It ended as: "Tercero, soy vegetariano: no soy exigente, solo no como carne; ojalá la familia pueda preparar algo para mí."
   What was wrong: 1. 'Espero que' still presents the family's cooking as something he expects of them, which a host-family reader may hear as a demand. It also assumes a host family, though the housing choice is still open.
2. The English aside is unreadable for the Spanish reader and sits in the middle of the Spanish sentence. The reader cannot tell whether he is not fussy about food or has other restrictions.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: ojalá: 'Espero que' sounds like you expect the family to cook, which a host reader can hear as a demand. 'Ojalá' with 'pueda' turns it into a soft wish: you hope they can, and it is still clear that you would like it. Written as 'espero que la familia tenga que cocinar' it would sound like a requirement.
3. They first wrote: "Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes porque tengo que comprar el vuelo."
   It ended as: "Necesito que me responda antes de fin de mes, porque tengo que comprar el vuelo."
   What was wrong: 'Necesito una respuesta' states a demand for a reply by a deadline to a school contact, which reads as pressure. The reason is sound, but the wording tells her what to do and how fast.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: Necesito que me responda: The writer's 'necesito una respuesta' makes the reply the thing he orders, which sounds like a demand on her. 'Necesito que me responda' keeps the same firm need but puts it on her as the person who replies, which is politer. 'Responda' is the usted subjunctive, which 'que' requires.
4. They first wrote: "Mirando adelante a oír de usted."
   It ended as: "Quedo a la espera de sus noticias."
   What was wrong: This is an English 'looking forward to hearing from you' rendered word for word. A Spanish reader does not recognise the closing phrase and may find it odd at the end of a formal letter.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: Quedo a la espera de: This is the standard Spanish closing for a formal letter. "Mirando adelante a" is a word-for-word copy of "looking forward to", and Spanish readers don't use it. Quedar + a la espera de is the phrase they expect here. / sus noticias: In Spanish letters you hear from someone by getting their noticias, not by hearing (oír) from them. Compare "tener noticias suyas" or "sus noticias". "Oír de usted" would sound like a phone call. / sus: Keep the formal possessive to match usted. "Tus noticias" would switch to the tú register in the middle of a letter to a stranger.
5. They first wrote: "Vengo por mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy excitado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   It ended as: "Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy emocionado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   What was wrong: por → a: "Vengo por mejorar" would read as if "por" meant "because of"; "venir a + infinitive" is the normal way to say you come in order to do something.
   How: the tutor corrected it
6. They first wrote: "Vengo por mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy excitado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   It ended as: "Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy emocionado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   What was wrong: excitado → emocionado: "Excitado" in Spanish can mean sexually aroused, which would embarrass the reader. "Emocionado" gives the intended eagerness.
   How: the tutor corrected it
7. They first wrote: "Tercero, soy vegetariano (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat) y espero que la familia puede cocinar algo para mí."
   It ended as: "Tercero, soy vegetariano (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat) y espero que la familia pueda cocinar algo para mí."
   What was wrong: puede → pueda: "Espero que" requires the subjunctive, so the verb must be "pueda".
   How: the tutor corrected it
8. They first wrote: "Estoy seguro de que voy a tener un buen tiempo en su escuela."
   It ended as: "Estoy seguro de que voy a pasarlo muy bien en su escuela."
   What was wrong: tener un buen tiempo → pasarlo muy bien: "Tener un buen tiempo" is a calque of English "have a good time". The idiomatic Spanish is "pasarlo bien" or "pasarlo muy bien".
   How: the tutor corrected it

Their notebook keeps Spanish expressions to review later. For each part, first lesson: what the change teaches, in a few English words. Then file: whether it earns an entry. An entry is worth filing only when the change teaches a reusable Spanish expression this writer did not have: a word in the sense meant here, which verb, preposition or adjective goes with which word, a set phrase or formula, the way this community says something. Not worth filing: a grammar rule applied (agreement, tense, mood, articles, gender, word order, a missing verb), spelling, accents, punctuation and capitals, a fact or a name put right, one of the writer's own alternatives picked, and words a writer at their level already uses (judge their level from what the draft already gets right).
One entry per expression: when two parts teach the same one, file it with the first and not again.
For a part you file, write the entry:
- phrase: the expression the change taught: the words that do the job the change was about, not the sentence's frame around them; as a learner would file it, in the form a phrasebook lists it ("topped with", "it's not anyone's fault"), at most six words, "…" only where a slot really varies; no letters such as X or Y, no translation, no grammar terms.
- meaning: in English, one short line: what it means or does, in the sense it has here.
- usage: in English, one or two short sentences: when people use it and what it goes with (register when it matters), and what makes it better than what they first wrote when that is the point.
- examples: three short, natural Spanish sentences using it in exactly the sense it has here (if it has other senses, as "our own" means both "made by us" and "belonging to us", never those), each with its English translation (n): one in a situation like theirs (not their own sentence again), two in everyday situations far from it, built differently around it so they see how it is used, not one frame. Names of people, characters, places and groups stay exactly as the piece writes them, in the translations too (never a translated or transliterated name).
- ended: how it ended, copied exactly, with the expression as used there marked by a tag (<m>…</m>). In each example's t, mark the expression the same way.
Marking shows where the expression is in a sentence: the words of that sentence that are the expression, as they are inflected there, and not words that only fill a slot in it; when other words come between its parts, each part is marked on its own.
For a part you do not file, give only n, lesson and file.
The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.
Reply with JSON only: {"notes":[{"n":1,"lesson":"","file":true,"phrase":"","ended":"","meaning":"","usage":"","examples":[{"t":"","n":""}]},{"n":2,"lesson":"","file":false}]}

Spanish uses 'quedar' for location, so 'queda cerca de' is more natural than 'es cerca de', which copies the English 'is near'.","examples":[{"t":"¿Queda la residencia cerca de la universidad?","n":"Is the residence close to the university?"},{"t":"El supermercado queda cerca de mi casa.","n":"The supermarket is near my house."},{"t":"¿Dónde queda la estación? Creo que queda cerca de aquí.","n":"Where is the station? I think it's near here."}]},{"n":2,"lesson":"'Ojalá' with a subjunctive makes a request a soft wish, not an expectation.","file":true,"phrase":"ojalá pueda","ended":"y <m>ojalá</m> la familia <m>pueda</m> preparar algo para mí.","meaning":"I hope (someone) can; I'd like it if (someone) could.","usage":"Used to express a hopeful wish about what someone might do, softer than 'espero que', which can sound like an expectation or demand on the other person. Followed by the subjunctive.","examples":[{"t":"<m>Ojalá pueda</m> venir a la fiesta el sábado.","n":"I hope I can come to the party on Saturday."},{"t":"Llueve mucho, pero <m>ojalá</m> <m>pueda</m> salir un rato.","n":"It's raining a lot, but I hope I can go out for a while."},{"t":"<m>Ojalá</m> el tren <m>pueda</m> llegar a tiempo.","n":"I hope the train can arrive on time."}]},{"n":3,"lesson":"'Necesito que me responda' keeps the need but puts the action on her, which is politer.","file":false},{"n":4,"lesson":"'Quedo a la espera de sus noticias' is the standard Spanish closing for a formal letter.","file":true,"phrase":"quedo a la espera de","ended":"<m>Quedo a la espera de</m> sus noticias.","meaning":"I remain waiting for (something); I look forward to (someone's reply).","usage":"A set closing formula for formal letters and emails, used before 'sus noticias', 'su respuesta' or similar. The English 'looking forward to' does not translate word for word, and 'mirando adelante a' is not used by Spanish readers.","examples":[{"t":"<m>Quedo a la espera de</m> su confirmación.","n":"I look forward to your confirmation."},{"t":"<m>Quedo a la espera de</m> su pronta respuesta.","n":"I look forward to your prompt reply."},{"t":"<m>Quedamos a la espera de</m> que llegue el técnico.","n":"We are waiting for the technician to arrive."}]},{"n":5,"lesson":"'Venir a' plus an infinitive means coming in order to do something; 'por' would mean 'because of'.","file":true,"phrase":"venir a…","ended":"<m>Vengo a</m> mejorar mi español","meaning":"to come in order to (do something).","usage":"Used to say why you come somewhere, followed directly by an infinitive. 'Venir por' would suggest a reason or a person to fetch, so 'venir a' is the right pattern here.","examples":[{"t":"<m>Vengo a</m> visitar a mi familia.","n":"I come to visit my family."},{"t":"Mi hermana <m>viene a</m> cenar los jueves.","n":"My sister comes to have dinner on Thursdays."},{"t":"<m>Venimos a</m> recoger los documentos.","n":"We've come to collect the documents."}]},{"n":6,"lesson":"'Excitado' means sexually aroused in Spanish; 'emocionado' gives the intended eagerness.","file":true,"phrase":"estar emocionado de","ended":"<m>estoy</m> muy <m>emocionado de</m> aprender","meaning":"to be excited or eager about (doing something).","usage":"Used to say you are looking forward to something with positive eagerness. 'Excitado' is a false friend here and can sound embarrassing, so 'estar emocionado de' is the safe, natural choice.","examples":[{"t":"<m>Estoy emocionada de</m> ver la película mañana.","n":"I'm excited to see the film tomorrow."},{"t":"Los niños <m>están emocionados de</m> ir a la playa.","n":"The children are excited to go to the beach."},{"t":"<m>Estamos emocionados de</m> conocer tu ciudad.","n":"We're eager to get to know your city."}]},{"n":7,"lesson":"'Espero que' needs the subjunctive, so the verb must be 'pueda'.","file":false},{"n":8,"lesson":"'Pasarlo bien' is the idiomatic way to say 'have a good time', not 'tener un buen tiempo'.","file":true,"phrase":"pasarlo bien","ended":"voy a <m>pasarlo</m> muy <m>bien</m> en su escuela.","meaning":"to have a good time; to enjoy oneself.","usage":"The everyday way to say you will enjoy an experience. 'Tener un buen tiempo' is a calque of English 'have a good time' and sounds unnatural in Spanish. 'Muy' can go between 'pasarlo' and 'bien'.","examples":[{"t":"<m>Lo pasamos bien</m> en la fiesta.","n":"We had a good time at the party."},{"t":"¿<m>Lo pasaste bien</m> en el campamento?","n":"Did you have a good time at the camp?"},{"t":"Los niños <m>lo pasan</m> muy <m>bien</m> en la playa.","n":"The children have a really good time at the beach."}]}]}
